title: Direct identification of the child through transmitted account/device identifiers
description: When the child's device sends live GPS updates, the transmission is typically authenticated or tagged with an account ID, device ID, session token, or similar identifier. The act of sharing these identifiers together with precise location data can directly identify the child or single them out to the receiving system.
assumptions: Assumes the GPS update payload or associated protocol metadata contains a persistent or account-linked identifier.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement; exact sub-node may vary by the project's LINDDUN Pro catalog.

title: Disclosure of highly sensitive live location by the child device
description: The source discloses precise, continuous GPS coordinates. Live location data can reveal home, school, routines, religious attendance, health visits, and other sensitive aspects of the child's private life.
assumptions: Assumes coordinates are sufficiently precise and frequent to reconstruct movements and places visited.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node granularity may differ in the official threat tree; applicability is strong.

title: Linkability of successive GPS updates on the flow
description: Regular interval transmission of GPS coordinates over the same logical flow allows successive messages to be linked to the same child/device, enabling reconstruction of movement trajectories over time even if each individual coordinate seems innocuous in isolation.
assumptions: Assumes repeated updates carry a stable pseudonym, session context, network metadata, or are otherwise correlatable as belonging to the same sender.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the core linkability threat clearly applies.

title: Identifiability from network and protocol metadata in transit
description: Even in transit, metadata such as IP address, device identifiers, timing patterns, and persistent tokens can make the child or their device identifiable, especially when combined with precise location updates.
assumptions: Assumes ordinary network/protocol metadata is observable within the communication path or by the receiving endpoint.
uncertainty_note: Applies even if payload contents are protected, but exact exposure depends on transport protections and architecture.

title: Disclosure of location and movement patterns in transit
description: The data flow carries precise live GPS coordinates at regular intervals. If the flow is intercepted, insufficiently protected, or exposed through logs/proxies, it can disclose the child's current whereabouts and movement history.
assumptions: Assumes some realistic possibility of interception, endpoint logging, or intermediary exposure.
uncertainty_note: Likelihood depends strongly on transport security and operational controls.

title: Backend can link repeated location updates into a persistent movement profile
description: By receiving regular GPS updates, the backend can associate multiple observations with the same child over time, creating a longitudinal movement profile and linking visits, routines, and behaviors across contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores or can correlate updates per child/account/device.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the destination-side linkability threat is clear.

title: Backend can identify the child from precise location history
description: The backend may identify the child not only from explicit account identifiers but also from the uniqueness of their location traces, such as recurring home and school locations, making the child identifiable even under pseudonyms.
assumptions: Assumes the backend has access to account data or can infer identity from unique mobility patterns.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may differ; identifiability from location traces is well established.

title: Backend processing discloses sensitive private-life information from location data
description: Once received, the backend can infer sensitive information from the child's live and historical locations, including daily routines, social relationships, school attendance, religious practices, and visits to medical or counseling facilities.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores, analyzes, or otherwise processes the received coordinates beyond transient routing.
uncertainty_note: Strong applicability; exact tree-node numbering may vary.

title: Backend may use live GPS data for purposes unexpected by the child
description: The destination may process the child's continuous location stream for secondary purposes beyond the child's reasonable expectations, such as analytics, profiling, behavioral monitoring, or sharing with third parties, creating an unawareness threat.
assumptions: Assumes purposes, retention, or onward uses are not fully transparent to the child.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the actual notices and UX presented to the child; included as a plausible destination-side privacy threat.

title: Backend collection of a child's live location may exceed consent or legal basis
description: Continuous collection of a child's precise GPS coordinates may occur without valid, informed, age-appropriate consent/assent, parental authorization where required, or another proper legal basis, creating a non-compliance risk at the receiving system.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to child-privacy, data-protection, or ePrivacy-style obligations and that compliance controls may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and product context; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Backend stores precise location pings beyond what is necessary
description: The backend writes each location ping to persistent storage, which can constitute avoidable disclosure of highly sensitive personal data if full precision, full frequency, or all events are stored by default rather than only the minimum needed for the service purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the service may not require retention of every raw location ping at full granularity for all users.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for excessive collection/storage under Data Disclosure; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ; threat applicability is strong even if the precise node label is approximate.

description: On receipt, the backend may process and store invitation details, child association, and recipient contact information. If it exposes these details to internal staff, downstream services, analytics, or notification providers beyond what is necessary, the backend causes disclosure of sensitive family and location-sharing information.
assumptions: Backend stores invitation records and may integrate with messaging, analytics, customer-support, or audit systems.
uncertainty_note: Applies if backend-side access control, minimization, or segregation are insufficient; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Backend may use invitation data for purposes beyond enabling guardian access
description: The backend could repurpose recipient contact details, relationship information, or invitation events for analytics, growth, profiling, or marketing without the parent reasonably expecting such use. This creates a use beyond the original purpose of adding a secondary guardian.
assumptions: Invitation events and contact details are retained and available to product analytics or other secondary-use functions.
uncertainty_note: Depends on actual backend governance and privacy controls; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Backend processing of the secondary guardian's contact details may occur without adequate consent or legal basis
description: The backend receives and processes personal data about the invited guardian, such as email address or phone number, before that person has accepted the invitation. If the service lacks an appropriate legal basis, notice, or consent mechanism for this processing, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The invitation includes personal contact details of a non-user or not-yet-user secondary guardian.
uncertainty_note: Jurisdiction-specific legal basis may vary; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Backend may be unable to prove what invitation and authorization the parent actually initiated
description: If the backend does not keep adequate records of who invited whom, for which child, with what permissions, and when, disputes may arise about whether the parent authorized sharing with the secondary guardian. This undermines accountability for a sensitive sharing action.
assumptions: Invitation grants or leads to access to the child's location data and may later be disputed.
uncertainty_note: This is a privacy-relevant repudiation threat only if auditability is insufficient; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Backend discloses the child's live location to a secondary guardian beyond strict necessity or without valid authorization
description: The backend actively shares highly sensitive real-time location data about a child with the secondary guardian. If access is granted without robust authorization checks, appropriate parental consent, scope limitation, or need-to-know validation, this constitutes information disclosure caused by the source's act of sharing.
assumptions: Assumes the secondary guardian may not always be fully authorized for continuous live-location access, or authorization may be broader than necessary.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction/position but not detailed node mappings.

title: Live-location payload and flow metadata can identify the child and guardian relationship in transit
description: The data flow contains or implies highly identifying information: the child's precise live location, the fact that a secondary guardian is associated with that child, and timing/frequency of updates. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, the combination of recipient, timestamps, and location trajectory can identify the child or infer the guardian-child relationship.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries precise or frequent location updates and that transport metadata or payload contents are observable to some degree by intermediaries or logs.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate.

title: Repeated live-location updates enable linkability of the child's movements and association with the secondary guardian
description: Continuous or repeated location sharing allows observations across time to be linked into a movement profile. The flow itself also links the child to a specific secondary guardian account, enabling correlation of events, routines, and relationships across sessions or datasets.
assumptions: Assumes updates are recurring rather than one-off and can be correlated by identifiers, tokens, or stable communication patterns.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian may further disclose or misuse the child's live location after receipt
description: Once the secondary guardian receives the child's live location, privacy harm can arise at the destination if they store, reshare, screenshot, verbally disclose, or otherwise use the data beyond the intended safeguarding purpose. The destination's handling can therefore cause additional information disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the recipient can access, retain, or redistribute the received location information.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian can infer sensitive patterns and activities from live location
description: Real-time and historical location observations allow the recipient to infer sensitive information about the child, such as home and school addresses, routines, religious attendance, medical visits, social relationships, or custody patterns. These inferences arise from destination-side processing of the received data.
assumptions: Assumes the recipient can observe location over time or combine it with contextual knowledge.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate.

title: Granting secondary-guardian access without clear consent, transparency, or policy basis may violate privacy expectations
description: Sharing a child's live location with a secondary guardian may be non-compliant if the backend enables access without a valid legal basis, age-appropriate transparency, parental authorization, or adherence to data-minimization and purpose-limitation requirements. The source's decision to grant access creates the compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the system operates in a regulated context and that governance around secondary-guardian access may be incomplete or ambiguous.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate and depends on jurisdiction-specific obligations.

title: Sharing analytics may enable cross-context linkage by the partner
description: Even if described as aggregated usage and engagement analytics, the backend's act of disclosing recurring app, cohort, campaign, device-class, region, or timestamped metrics to the advertising/analytics partner can enable that partner to link this dataset with other datasets it already holds about the same app, publisher, campaign, or user segments. The privacy threat arises at the source because P1 initiates disclosure to a third party for monetization.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics contain stable dimensions, segment identifiers, campaign identifiers, timestamps, or other quasi-identifiers rather than only fully anonymized, one-off statistics.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Aggregated analytics may still disclose information about individuals or small groups
description: If the backend shares analytics with fine-grained breakdowns (e.g. by location, device type, feature usage, time window, or niche cohort), the disclosure itself can reveal personal or sensitive information about individuals or very small groups through singling out or inference, despite being labeled aggregated.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style minimum group sizes, suppression, or noise addition are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Applies strongly when cohorts can become small; if only coarse, privacy-preserving aggregates are shared, this threat may be reduced.

title: Backend may share analytics for advertising funding beyond users' reasonable expectations
description: Sending usage and engagement analytics to an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier may be unexpected from the user's perspective, especially if users perceive analytics as necessary for service operation rather than third-party monetization. The threat arises at the source because P1 decides to use the data for a potentially incompatible secondary purpose.
assumptions: Assumes users were not clearly informed that their app usage data would be shared with a third-party advertising/analytics partner for monetization, or that this purpose is broader than strictly necessary service analytics.
uncertainty_note: Purpose compatibility depends on the app's notices, consent flows, and jurisdictional requirements.

title: Third-party analytics sharing may occur without valid consent or other appropriate legal basis
description: Because the flow sends usage and engagement analytics to an external advertising/analytics partner for monetization, the backend may process and disclose personal data without valid, specific, and informed consent, or without another appropriate legal basis where required. The privacy threat arises at the source because P1 initiates the disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics remain personal data or pseudonymous data under applicable law, and that advertising/analytics sharing requires consent or another legal basis in the deployment context.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability varies by jurisdiction and by whether the data are truly anonymized.

title: Data in transit may identify the app, publisher, or user segments to the recipient or observers
description: During transmission, payload fields and metadata such as app identifier, partner account, campaign identifiers, region, device class, or segment labels can identify the app's user population or particular user segments. Even if direct identifiers are absent, in-transit metadata may make the subjects or source organization identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes the transfer includes descriptive metadata or payload dimensions beyond purely anonymous totals.
uncertainty_note: If transport is strongly protected and payloads are minimized, this risk is lower; tree-node id is best-effort.

title: Transmission metadata can support linkage across reports and datasets
description: Repeated transfers of analytics reports over this flow can expose stable metadata patterns such as schedule, account identifiers, campaign IDs, schema fields, or segment labels. These in-transit characteristics can help the partner or an interceptor correlate multiple reports and link them to other datasets.
assumptions: Assumes recurring transfers with stable identifiers or schemas.
uncertainty_note: If reports are one-off, heavily aggregated, and sent over well-protected channels with minimal metadata, this threat is reduced.

title: Partner can link received analytics with its broader advertising datasets
description: Once received, the advertising/analytics partner may combine the analytics with its existing advertiser, publisher, campaign, SDK, or cross-app datasets, enabling linkage of app usage patterns to broader profiles or segments. The threat arises at the destination because EE4 performs the combining and analysis.
assumptions: Assumes EE4 has other datasets and contractual or technical ability to correlate them with the received analytics.
uncertainty_note: This is especially plausible for large analytics/ad-tech partners; exact linkage capability depends on the partner.

title: Partner may infer sensitive traits or behaviors from received analytics
description: The partner can analyze engagement and usage analytics to derive insights about user groups, such as interests, routines, demographics, or potentially sensitive behaviors, even when the data are aggregated. The privacy threat arises at the destination because EE4 performs the inference.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics include sufficiently granular dimensions, time series, or segment breakdowns to support inference.
uncertainty_note: Inference risk depends heavily on granularity and whether the partner already has auxiliary data.

title: Partner may reuse analytics for broader advertising or profiling purposes
description: After receipt, the partner may use the analytics not only to provide reporting but also to optimize ad targeting, enrich profiles, benchmark publishers, or support other commercial analytics purposes that go beyond the original user-facing expectation. This constitutes use for potentially incompatible secondary purposes at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes contractual restrictions do not fully prohibit such reuse, or enforcement is weak.
uncertainty_note: Actual reuse depends on the partner agreement and technical controls.

title: Partner processing may be non-compliant with consent, transparency, or data-sharing obligations
description: At receipt, the external partner may process the analytics in ways that do not satisfy applicable privacy obligations, such as honoring consent scope, providing adequate transparency, respecting purpose limitation, or meeting controller/processor data-sharing requirements.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics are still personal data or can affect identifiable persons or groups under applicable law.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction, roles of the parties, and whether the data are truly anonymized.

description: The child shares current location as part of the SOS/check-in. Location data is highly privacy-sensitive and reveals where the child is at that moment.

title: Attributable evidence that the child sent an SOS/check-in
description: The SOS/check-in message can serve as evidence that this specific child initiated the communication at a particular time and place, reducing the child's ability to later deny having sent it.

title: Linkability of repeated SOS/check-in events on the data flow
description: Repeated transmissions on this flow may be linkable via persistent identifiers, account identifiers, device identifiers, network metadata, or stable communication patterns, allowing multiple events to be linked to the same child over time.

description: The data flow carries the child's current location and the fact that an SOS/check-in occurred. If exposed in transit, this reveals sensitive whereabouts and potentially that the child is in distress or under supervision.

description: By receiving the message, the backend gains access to the child's current location and the fact that a manual check-in/SOS was triggered, which are sensitive personal data points.

description: Receiving and processing a child's precise location and SOS/check-in may trigger heightened legal and policy obligations, such as child-data protections, purpose limitation, minimization, retention limits, and transparency requirements.
